articles.title: The Pixel 11 Pro is a great phone, no thanks to its flashiest new features
articles.summary: Forget HiLight and Proactive Assistance. The Pixel 11 Pro is at its best with focused new tools that actually work.
articles.body: Google is trying to get you off your phone. The Pixel 11 Pro is “A Phone Designed to Help You Use It Less,” the company promises. It can proactively help you book restaurant reservations, take the best frames from a video, and help you voice-text significantly faster. The pitch is that the new features bundled with the Pixel 11 series of phones can help fix your relationship with technology — one that Google knows has badly degraded in recent years. But the hardware of the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL is very similar to last year’s models — and in at least one case, a downgrade — so those software features are pretty much the entire pitch.  Over the last week testing the 11 Pro, I’ve been trying them all to see how much they can help me put my phone down. Like many experiences with Google software, when they work, they are genuinely helpful. But getting them to work often requires a very narrow set of circumstances that some Google engineer probably dreamed up in the “society if” utopia lab. [Product: Google Pixel 11 Pro | [Product: Google Pixel 11 Pro XL | The Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL are minor hardware updates compared to last year’s Pixel 10 Pro and 10 Pro XL. They both get brighter 3,600-nit screens. Their charging has been upgraded, with faster wired speeds and Qi2.2 for up to 25W when wireless. The 5x optical telephoto camera has a bigger sensor that Google says enables 30 percent more light intake. Storage now starts at 256GB, instead of 128GB. And there’s also a fancy new “notification light,” which I’ll get to in a bit.  Unfortunately, these upgrades come with a downgrade too, for the base model at least. The 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL now start with less RAM: 12GB compared to the 16GB that came standard last year, the same amount as the regular Pixel 11. I’m testing the 16GB / 512GB model, so unfortunately I can’t tell you if the RAM decrease is noticeable. That base model is also $100 more expensive than last year, too, at $1,099.   With such minor spec changes, Google has gone all in on software this year. And this time, that software’s primary purpose is to get you off your phone, or at least get tedious tasks done faster so you can get back to your life. [Image: Proactive Assistance popping up inside Google Messages. Perhaps the largest push in this direction is the Pixel 11’s new “Proactive Assistance” feature. This is a set of dynamic chips that appear when certain interactions happen on your phone, like a friend asking what your schedule looks like next week or if you booked that table at a restaurant yet. For the most basic interactions, like checking availability or adding an event to my calendar, I found Proactive Assistance really helpful. I practically live inside my calendar, and text conversations about scheduling are common. When my friend Marc texted me asking when I was available next week, Gemini popped up and suggested checking my calendar for times. Outside of simple scenarios like that, though, Proactive Assistance gets less reliable. One of Google’s key examples is letting Gemini book a dinner reservation for you if you’re chatting about heading out to eat, but I had to receive a text with an extremely specific string of information to get it to work — and even then it only worked sometimes. For example, receiving the text “Can you make a reservation at Frankie Spuntino next Saturday at 7pm?” surfaced a chip to agentically try to make the reservation. But if the message doesn’t include the date or time, it won’t invoke anything at all. Most of the time when the chip does show up, it disappears the moment I reply. Occasionally it will stick around if the AI thinks we’re still talking about the restaurant, but those instances were few and far between. I wish Google would keep the chip around for at least a few messages, or have it float around the messages in some way. One promise of large language models is the ability to understand what you mean and remove the requirements for smart keywords, so it’s odd that explicit keywords are still necessary to get so much of Proactive Assistance to work. I can see what Google is trying to do with this and I can maybe see a future where it gets refined, but as it stands, it’s simply too inconsistent. Plus, I had to manually toggle on Proactive Assistance and add OpenTable to connected apps in settings, which I just don’t think most people will know to do. As my colleague Cameron Faulkner puts it, “You need to be proactive to get Proactive Assistance to work.” Proactive Assistance is advertised as working with other scenarios too, like surfacing your flight information when someone asks what time your flight is or bringing up the right photo when someone asks for it. But both of these scenarios either failed or were inconsistent for me. Asking when my flight is supposed to land surfaced nothing even though I have flight information in my Gmail, and when my friend asked for a photo of me from 2024, it surfaced photos from 2024, but none of me. It’s disappointing that this feature only works in such narrow circumstances. I can see the vision, but the execution just isn’t there yet. [Image: The HiLight LED. Another feature that got a lot of marketing hype but flatlined on its delivery is HiLight. You may have noticed the temperature sensor is missing on the Pixel 11 Pro. Instead, Google has replaced it with a multicolored LED ring hidden inside the flash that can glow when different things are happening on your phone. Again, in concept, I love this idea. Google wants you to be living your life, with your phone placed face down on the table so it can’t distract you unless HiLight notifies you of something you need to pay attention to. In practice, HiLight is so badly executed that it’s frankly embarrassing. Right now, HiLight can glow for exactly two things. First, it will glow and animate when you’re speaking with Gemini, but only while your phone is face down on the table. These are two things I do not do very often. When I use Gemini, I’m generally typing to it, and when I do use Gemini voice mode, my phone is in my hand or sitting screen up. If this was just one of the many things HiLight could light up for, I wouldn’t find it so offensive. But at the moment, the only other thing HiLight will glow for is for calls from your favorite contacts. I wish I was kidding. [Image: The only options for HiLight. If I’m getting a call from a favorite contact, I just want my phone to ring. Again, if it was just an additional feature, then sure, I guess. I don’t mind having an additional indicator that a favorite is calling me while my phone is face down. But if the call is coming through anyway, it’s really not that much effort to turn the phone over and see who it is. To make it worse, you can only choose from five colors, and one of them is white! Customizable RGB LEDs were a feature we lost long ago, but when we did have it, it was almost always possible to map to just about any notification you wanted: red for a new email, green for a WhatsApp message. Google has confirmed that it’s looking to add text notifications from favorite contacts to HiLight, but why not just make it customizable to any app? This feels like such a missed opportunity, and it’s wild to me that it wasn’t better thought out before launch. Right now, it’s just acting like my flash, like it’s always been. There are some new features that I’m finding genuinely useful that do help me stay in the moment, though. I was most pleasantly surprised by Rambler, a souped-up voice-to-text tool powered by Gemini. Rambler removes the filler words that voice-to-text would normally pick up, does proper grammar and punctuation without explicitly asking for it, and will even rewrite misspeaks mid-recording. The speed of the Pixel’s voice-to-text has been one of its strong suits ever since Google started using its own Tensor chips on the Pixel 6, but Rambler makes this even better, to the point where I’m dictating the text on my phone whenever I have the opportunity. It is a genuinely great feature, saves me time, and almost makes it feel like I’m having a conversation in real time while texting. [Image: Using Rambler on the Pixel 11 Pro. As is tradition, Google also introduced a bunch of new camera features this year, and perhaps the most prominent is Magic Capture. The feature is front and center in the camera app right next to the photo and video modes, which tells you something about how confident Google is in it. Start a Magic Capture, point it at what’s happening, and when you’re done recording, Gemini will do some processing and pull out what it considers the best photos and video clips from the session. During the Made by Google keynote last week, Google demoed the feature by recording some people shooting hoops on a basketball court. In the demonstration, Google said you could simply hold your phone and let it record while you take in the moment with your eyes. I have tried this exact scenario quite a few times, and let me tell you, it is extremely difficult to keep your subject in frame if you’re not staring at your screen. Magic Capture did a great job of pulling relevant images and clips from my recordings when I was making sure to keep my subject in frame by, you know, staring at my screen, but unless you have your phone mounted on a tripod or something, it’s naive to think you can ignore your phone completely. That caveat aside, I really like this feature. I take a lot of videos on my phone, but I’m much more likely to revisit pictures. With Magic Capture, I can have both. The main caveat seems to be that stabilization isn’t as good on the clips it cuts compared to clips you’d take in video mode. Even so, I think Magic Capture will be useful for parents trying to capture moments of their kids, without needing to work so hard to get the perfect smile for a photo. Instead of marketing this feature as something that lets you be in the moment by not looking at your phone at all, it would probably be better to pitch it as something that will automatically grab great photos and short video clips for you, and all you need to do is point your phone and hit record. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: While Magic Capture took most of the spotlight in Google’s keynote, maybe the most discussed photo upgrade this year is Camera Looks. I did a whole interview with Google’s camera chief about this feature going deep into how the new system was made, and there’s a lot of potential in the execution. Camera Looks is a new photography feature you can think of similar to Fujifilm’s film simulations, which let its cameras emulate different film styles on the JPGs they put out. On the Pixel 11 series, there are four modifications of the standard camera, with Original, Natural, Shadows, and Vanilla giving subtle tweaks to your image. But if you want to get more out there, there are six additional creative looks, called Editorial, Velvet, Classic, Digi, Black Tie, and Minimal. Each of the looks can be modified to your liking, with adjustable settings like contrast, highlights, shadows, vibrance, tint, warmth, sharpness, and grain. What makes this a really interesting feature to me is that Google is adjusting the amount of computational processing it’s doing at capture, based on the settings you choose; it’s not just applying filters later. For example, the Digi mode will do less frame stacking and the Minimal mode will apply less sharpness and contrast. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: I really dig the looks, even right out of the box. They span from basic edits to quite inspired, and if you’re looking for something that gives you the “film simulation look” straight out of camera, these definitely deliver. It was high time Google added some more creative looks to the Pixel, especially considering it doesn’t have nearly as robust a third-party camera ecosystem as the iPhone. I’ve personally made the Minimal mode permanent on my phone for its unsharpened, minimally contrasty look, occasionally switching to Classic, but after testing them all, I think Velvet and Editorial will get a lot of use, since they have the most “film aesthetic” of the bunch. With less processed photos, you can actually see texture in photos, which is normally washed away by noise reduction algorithms. Overall camera quality on the Pixel 11 Pro series is great this year, and practically the only reason to pick up a Pro Pixel over the standard 11, aside from wanting a larger phone, in the case of the XL. The primary sensor is technically new, but Google tells me it’s the same size as last year and was swapped in because it uses slightly less power. The biggest camera hardware change is the new larger telephoto sensor, which Google says captures more light, and I can tell. Telephoto cameras are usually the weakest link in a smartphone’s camera arsenal, but even at 10x zoom, which is a 2x crop of the telephoto sensor, it was hard to notice any significant quality degradation. Plus, the transition between sensors is much smoother now, with only a very slight jump when switching between lenses. [Image: The Camera Looks interface. The Pixel 11 Pro also includes a 120x Pro Zoom mode, enabled by the new image signal processor in Tensor G6. Like the 100x Pro Zoom on the Pixel 10 Pro, Google is using generative AI to upscale your highly zoomed-in images to make them look more realistic. On objects without a lot of sharp edges this actually does a pretty good job, and Google will give you both the non-AI-enhanced and enhanced versions so you can see the difference. I was in Spain during last week’s solar eclipse, and the Pixel 11 Pro did a good job of turning a zoomed-in photo of the moon from a blurry mess into something that looked good enough to elicit responses of awe when I posted it in Slack. But that was a relatively simple image, and shots with a lot more detail often look like an early AI-generated image, with skewed angles and edges, garbled text, and muddy tones. I’d only really use this if you needed to see information you can’t see with your normal eyes, not for artistic purposes. [Image: [Image: The Pixel 11 Pro also gets a new, faster Night Sight, which Google says is about three times faster on average than the Pixel 10 Pro. In testing, most Night Sight images I took only needed to be held for one second, and I got all the same benefits you got from holding the phone for three or more seconds previously. This is the kind of quality-of-life update I love to see, and I’m glad Google is continuing to improve here. I love Rambler, Magic Capture, and Camera Looks. If you’re looking to upgrade your phone this year, they’re legitimately great features. But after a week of use, it’s clear to me that the Pixel 11 Pro is not yet smart enough to help me use my phone less, despite what Google claims. Proactive Assistance is only bound to save you a few seconds and a few taps compared to just opening the apps and doing the steps yourself. If you were hoping for the Pixel 11 Pro would help address your phone addiction, that’s probably not going to happen. But if you’re looking for a phone with the best voice-to-text on the market, great cameras with good built-in style, and solid hardware, the Pixel 11 Pro delivers.  Photography by David Imel / The Verge

articles.title: Somehow, Despite Being the Sixth Film in the Franchise, Insidious: Out of the Further Delivers a Popcorn-Rattling Ride Full of Fun, Creative Scares
articles.summary: Insidious: Out of the Further delivers a popcorn-rattling ride full of fun, creative scares and serviceable human stakes that more than justify tiptoeing through the tulips back to the spirit world.
articles.body:
Insidious: Out of the Further is in theaters on Friday, August 21.

With 2023’s Insidious: The Red Door having served as an effective swan song to Blumhouse’s first original horror franchise, Out of the Further arrives with one chance to prove that the light over the series’ spectral crimson door deserves to be kept on after all. With a grab bag of different-flavored scares that broadly work, some grounded performances, and a willingness to double down on the abject weirdness of the world-building that’s been established up to this point, against the odds for a sixth film in any franchise, Insidious: Out of the Further maintains a steady stride and winds up being a hell of a good time.

As the title suggests, Insidious: Out of the Further sets itself apart from the films which precede it by opening the proverbial (and literal) door from the spirit realm into the material plane in a much more significant way than ever before. It’s true that we’ve seen the spirits of the Further out in the real world, but generally, these apparitions are fairly closely shackled to the bodies of those they’re trying to possess, and incapable of too much more than going “boo”... or I guess luring them into the street, like in the case of Insidious: Chapter 3 ’s Quinn. The particulars of how (and to what degree) the Further gets Out are fun to discover along the way, but suffice to say that protagonist Gemma (Amelia Eve) had a rough childhood that has left her unable to move on in life in a way that’s made her a valuable target for the spirits of The Further. The opening scene paints a truly sad picture of Gemma’s childhood, as she tiptoes around her house to avoid drawing the attention of her mother, who’s clearly in the throes of a crisis that’s been going on for some time. It sets up a dynamic that carries into Gemma’s adulthood, as she navigates fears of transferring that experience onto her daughter Maya (Island Austin).

Amelia Eve does fine work shouldering Gemma’s growing instability as she tries to keep her feet on the ground, although writer/director Jacob Chase’s script hammers a bit too hard on the “passing familial trauma along” element of the story, routinely saying out loud what the imagery and performance already clearly communicate. It feels especially repetitive in the context of Insidious: The Red Door’s plot, which focused on the reconciliation of Patrick Wilson and Ty Simpkins’ Josh and Dalton Lambert after their shared experiences in the first two chapters of the series. Though it’s not always subtle, Chase does at least prioritize threading that family drama through Out of the Further in a way that keeps the central wound Gemma is nursing in focus, so that her desperation remains palpable throughout. We see the past repeating itself through Maya’s eyes as Gemma unravels, and Island Austin strikes a good balance between vulnerability and tenacity through her mom’s ups and downs.

Given all the new facets of how the Further is able to interact with the material plane in this film, Chase is able to stage a number of creative and fresh scenarios that delight in blurring the line between what’s happening in reality and what’s bleeding over from the spirit realm. Chase knows the Insidious films well, capably easing into the visual language of the series while also having a keen sense of how the rhythms of encounters with the denizens of the Further are expected to play out. At worst, the scares work about as well as they have in any other Insidious film (jump scares and audio stings abound), but Chase brings no shortage of new ideas to the table.

Two strong back-to-back sequences around the film’s midpoint represent Out of the Further at its best. The first is a claustrophobic’s nightmare set in Maya’s pillow fort. As Gemma pokes her head in, the pillow fort becomes a rat’s maze in which she’s very much not alone. Chase is able to draw the tension out of every wrong turn through the labyrinth very effectively, including some fun misdirects and camera coverage that make the most out of the tight space. By the time Gemma finally emerges, the viewer should feel just as relieved as the character.

But it’s the following sequence, which follows Gemma to her job as a dental hygienist, that is Out of the Further’s crown jewel. For a franchise that has always forefronted spectral spookies and haunted house-style bumps in the night, Insidious: Out of the Further features one of the more disgusting and visceral dental horror scenes I can recall ever having seen, as Gemma goes to work on a guy who seems like he may be better off getting his teeth checked by the Lipstick Face Demon from the first movie. Chase draws this sequence out to a fever pitch, layering one sickening and all-too-realistic gag over another. All that really dampens this excellent sequence is how it tails off into the Further, where evil-looking dentists and patients seem far more tame than the actual oral horror we just witnessed out in the real world.

The Insidious films have favored vague, elemental demons as antagonists up to this point, really as more of a visual focal point for the sleepless evil contained in the Further, but Out of the Further makes the smart choice to try out a more well-drawn villain this time out, played by A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms’ Sam Spruell. Cyrus Lam is no hoofed, red-faced Beelzebub, but a cunning spirit with an interesting backstory which connects to how much more interaction the Further and the real world have this time out. Cyrus and his motives aren’t all that deep, but he’s different enough from previous antagonists to make his moves feel a lot more unpredictable.

Out of the Further’s strength at delivering on that namesake concept does belie a weakness of the film’s, which is that most of the material set in the Further itself is rather forgettable. The space tends to be a VFX-darkened/color-graded void in the shape of whatever house or neighborhood that particular movie is set in, where the spirits have greater power. On that front, we’re pretty firmly in “been there, done that” territory. Die-hards will no doubt delight in the myriad familiar faces among the vaudevillian freakshow of ghouls that call the Further home, but with the stakes of the film being so focused on preventing the Further from getting out, much of the anxiety surrounding the idea of the characters being trapped within feels too distant for those moments to feel all that weighty.

The movie’s supporting cast are uniformly strong at keeping Insidious: Out of the Further from astral projecting itself into incoherence. Is there anything new for Lin Shaye’s Elise Rainier to do here other than amend exposition from previous movies to explain new abilities, raise a lantern in the darkness of the Further, and scream at ghosts in the face after dying five movies ago? Nope. Is her presence and personality as welcome and warm a blanket as ever? You betcha. As Gemma’s boyfriend Nick, Brandon Perea and his excellent comedic timing are particularly well-deployed as a very open-minded skeptic. Legends of Tomorrow’s Maisie Richardson-Sellers stops by as tattoo artist/medium Clare to pick up the torch from Elise in the material plane, and while she’s mostly there as a conduit for Elise, it’s easy to see her steely comfort with the abnormal becoming a more prominent part of the series going forward. And a special shoutout to the pair of actors who play Gemma’s neighbors, the O’Sullivans. They (with some canny direction on Chase’s part) absolutely nail a self-referential gag during the very intense finale and give me hope that, for every 10 or 12 poe-faced entities that reoccur from previous movies in future installments, we get one appearance from these two just doing their best to be helpful and not to bicker too much while doing so.

articles.title: Xbox Special Edition Translucent Green Controller Price, Release Date Leaked
articles.summary: Pricing and launch details for Microsoft's snazzy translucent green Xbox controller have leaked online.
articles.body:
Pricing and launch details for Microsoft's snazzy translucent green Xbox controller have leaked online.

Inspired by the iconic OG Xbox console, the Xbox Wireless Controller Special Edition X25 will launch on October 20, 2026 priced at $79.99 / £74.99 / €79.99, according to Dealabs ' ever-reliable billbil-kun.

Microsoft will reportedly make these details official next week at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany, with preorders set to go live on August 26. As yet, however, there's no word on the X25 Special Edition Xbox Series X — or at least, not word that has leaked.

The 25 Best Original Xbox Games of All Time

Xbox announced its limited-edition Xbox Series X console variant inspired by the original Xbox back in June, in celebration of the brand's 25th anniversary.

The console and controller both sport a translucent green shell, allowing you to see all of the inner-workings of the machine and its pad. As you might expect, the console will come bundled with a matching controller, as well as the pad being able to buy separately. The console itself is expected to launch sometime this November.

Xbox does not appear to be holding a dedicated press conference at Gamescom, but will hold two days of livestreams showing off its extensive slate of upcoming titles in detail. Expect a look at games such as Gears of War: E-Day, Minecraft Dungeons 2, and Fable on Wednesday, August 26. The following day, updates for Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, plus Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 and much more will be discussed.

As for big new surprises... perhaps we'll see some pop up in the event's main Opening Night Live showcase? As ever, IGN will be reporting on that live next Tuesday, August 25.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: Latest Xbox Console Updates Include Extremely Belated Profile Badge if You Bought an Xbox One Back in 2013
articles.summary: New Xbox console features include a special profile badge if you forked out for an Xbox One on day one back in November 2013.
articles.body:
New Xbox console features include a special profile badge if you forked out for an Xbox One on day one back in November 2013.

Microsoft has detailed its latest system updates coming to Xbox Series X/S consoles, including improvements to your home and game library screens, plus more control over your local game saves.

Perhaps most surprising is an extremely belated profile badge to owners of the Xbox One "Day One" achievement, which you could unlock by buying Microsoft's then-new console back in 2013. As someone who did indeed do this, I remember redeeming the product code on a piece of paper included in the box to get my 0 Gamerscore achievement that confirmed I had indeed purchased Microsoft's least beloved console generation. And now it is displayed on my Xbox profile, too!

This addition comes amid a refresh for profile badges in general, which now display high-resolution artwork and a description for each.

Perhaps more usefully, you can now further customize your Xbox's home screen by removing items from the recent games and apps list, including the Play History tile. There's a cool-looking immersive background mode, too, that you can enter via the R3 button on your controller. This effectively hides all Home UI elements, allowing your background to take center stage.

If you're looking to free up some hard drive space, another new option lets you browse your local game saves and remove any taking up too much room. They're all in the cloud, anyway! Removing local copies will tidy up hard drive space and just prompt a quick download of the cloud version the next time you load up your game.

Last but not least, purchased games will now be removed from your purchase wishlist. Handy!

All of these features will begin rolling out to Xbox owners today, though most will arrive slowly, and to Xbox Insiders first as they are bug-tested and approved for wider rollout.

Which are you most looking forward to? And are there any other Xbox One day one owners in the house?

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: GTA VI keeps leaking ahead of its gameplay premiere
articles.summary: Clips of what appears to be Grand Theft Auto VI have hit the internet, possibly spoiling aspects of the game ahead of Rockstar Games’ deep dive. Some clips have already been pulled.
articles.body: Clips of what appears to be Grand Theft Auto VI have hit the internet, possibly spoiling aspects of the game ahead of Rockstar Games’ deep dive debuting on Netflix next week and its long-awaited launch in November. I’ve seen three clips seemingly showing off the game, though two have been pulled from the site I saw them on “due to a copyright claim.” The first clip (now removed) was a quiet scene that mostly focused on Jason Duval, one the game’s two protagonists, shooting a basketball into a hoop. Another clip (also removed) featured more of the crime-focused gameplay you’d expect from GTA, including Duval hitting a person with a wrench, and also showed the return of a six-star Wanted system. A third clip, which is live as I write this, shows Duval driving at night, punching some people, using a taser, and stealing a truck. The clip then jumps to what looks like a cutscene from a different part of the game in the daytime. The videos were watermarked by a person or group identifying themselves as “CyberLeek.” The third clip has a call for viewers to buy a CyberLeek cryptocurrency, a QR code, links to some sketchy-looking CyberLeek URLs, and a statement that says “NO PHYSICAL DISCS? THEN MORE LEEKS!”, which is seemingly a reference to Rockstar’s decision not to launch GTA VI on a physical disc. This isn’t the first time apparent footage from GTA VI has leaked. In 2022, 90 videos leaked online long before the game’s official reveal more than a year later (a reveal that also leaked, leading Rockstar to publish the game’s first trailer a day early). A teen who played a key role in leaking the 90 videos was sentenced to life in a secure hospital. Rockstar also confirmed earlier this year that it had data compromised in a hack of a third-party provider, but said the incident would have “no impact on our organization or our players.” Rockstar and owner Take-Two didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. The GTA VI “extended look” premieres on Netflix on August 27th at 3PM ET and will stream on YouTube at 9PM ET. The $79.99 title is scheduled to launch on November 19th, and for the most part, the industry is steering clear of November and launching their big games earlier in the year.

articles.title: The Witcher 3 NPCs Kept Dropping Their Babies Due to an Unintended Side Effect of a Cut Mechanic
articles.summary: The Witcher 3 developers were so focused on making a realistic environment for players that they accidentally created a morbidly hilarious side effect for the game’s female NPCs.
articles.body:
The Witcher 3 developers were so focused on making a realistic environment for players that they accidentally created a morbidly hilarious side effect for the game’s female NPCs.

In an interview with Edge Magazine , CD Projekt Red quest designer Philipp Weber opened up about the unintended consequences of this strategy, saying the team was so honed in on creating a believable world that they ended up causing chaos, instead.

Weber explained that they wanted to give NPCs authentic behaviors to increase immersion and reward players for exploring the nooks and crannies of The Continent, particularly where small villages in the countryside were concerned.

"Because we were focused on the countryside, it was easier for players to become curious," he began. "If a village only has eight houses, people will want to see if the people truly exist in the world, or if it's just fakery. Lots of people nowadays are interested in those kinds of details, and it really came to haunt us."

At the time, Weber said the dev team was "more focused on simulating their proper day and night cycle" for these NPCs rather than giving them believable reactions to Geralt as he wandered around their world. “When it came to actually reacting to the player, there wasn't that much detail,” he admitted.

This meant that, although the NPCs had their own highly-specific schedules that made them seem like living, breathing people going about their daily lives, they weren’t exactly logical when it came to Geralt barging into their homes and swinging his weapons around.

"They would drop what they're currently working on, that thing would fall to the ground, and they'd run away, afraid,” Weber said.

Unfortunately (or fortunately, since it’s objectively funny) those ‘things’ included babies, which female characters would throw to the floor as they fled from danger. "For a few weeks, women were just dropping their babies, left and right,” he said.

While this problem ended up getting solved, it would have been absolutely wild to see in the final product. Weber shed a bit more light on their strategy when making NPCs in general, saying that rather than giving them specfic instructions, they're able to choose from certain "spots of interest."

"Most NPCs in villages, we don't give them specific paths," he explained. "We give them spots of interest that are available and then they're the ones doing the pathfinding: 'Once I'm done with woodcutting, I'll choose another point, and maybe do carpentry in front of my house'. For the 50 sailors at Novigrad harbour, for example, we made 200 possible spots, so even if all 50 were active at the same time, they would have options."

The next entry in the Witcher series is currently in development. Centering on Ciri, it does not yet have an official release date, but early gameplay footage was shown off for the State of Unreal 2025 showcase. We can’t imagine NPCs will be tossing their babies in this game, either, but you never know. (It certainly wouldn't be wilder than the 'put the baby in the oven' option.)

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

articles.title: Wolverine: Origin III Explores Marvel's Controversial Prequel Arc
articles.summary: Marvel is wading into controversial waters again with Wolverine: Origin III - The Dark Age, the latest chapter in the dramatic origin story of the iconic X-Man.
articles.body:
Before the release of 2001's Wolverine: Origin, it was unthinkable that Marvel would ever reveal the full background and origin story of the enigmatic man known as Logan. That book revealed Wolverine's true name (James Howlett) and explored the tragic series of events that led to him becoming an orphaned loner. It also directly inspired the 2009 movie X-Men Origins: Wolverine. Now Marvel is continuing that controversial saga with a third chapter called Wolverine: Origin III - The Dark Age.

Wolverine: Origin III - The Dark Age brings back original Origin writer Paul Jenkins. The series is illustrated by CAFU (Venom). Issue #1 features a main cover by Wes Burt and a variant cover by Josemaria Casanovas.

Origin III jumps further ahead in the Marvel timeline. Whereas the original was set in late 19th century Canada and 2013's Origin II was set in the early 20th century, Origin III takes place after World War II. After years spent waging war, Logan has finally found some semblance of peace, but will his past come back to haunt him?

Enter the Dark Age! After years of trauma and back-to-back tours of duty fighting in the first two World Wars, Logan has found his new mission…peace! With his berserker rage and violent tendencies somehow behind him, Logan enjoys a new life of tranquility and service. Logan will meet new friends and allies, and with the help of an impassioned young doctor, discover what makes him tick. But what is the cause of this newfound happiness…and how long can it last?

“Wolverine: Origin was foundational. It did not simply tell us how, why, and where a young, frail Canadian named James Howlett became the super hero we know as Wolverine, it also showed his loss of innocence and his understanding of a cruel and difficult world,” said Jenkins in a statement. “Now, after 25 years, I’m privileged to present this story I have waited over a quarter of a century to tell. Where did Logan go? Which parts of his story were lost to history? What led to the events of Weapon X? The answers are not going to be what you expect.”

Look for Wolverine: Origin III - The Dark Age to hit stores on December 16. You can preorder a copy at your local comic shop .

articles.title: What to Expect at IFA 2026: AI Is the Name of the Game
articles.summary: Not just a trade show; more like a cultural playground.
articles.body:
Editor's Note: This article is sponsored by IFA 2026. It has been updated with key points on August 18.

IFA 2026 is coming back soon and is set to take the world by storm. The event will highlight how “the future is now” in the realms of AI, smart homes, digital health, robotics, and much more. At IFA 2024, IGN was excited to see Acer announce the Nitro Blaze 7, its own contender to Steam Deck OLED and the Asus ROG Ally X. And in 2025, we saw a ton of home tech reveals from the likes of Eufy and Anker, with Eufy's new MarsWalker robot vacs and UV printers, and Anker's new Soundcore Nebula X1 Pro not-so-portable high-end projector. (It comes on wheels and boasts 3,500 ANSI lumens versus its portable Nebula Capsule that hits a max of 300 lumens, with Dolby surround sound to boot.)

That said, there is a lot of excitement in store for IFA this year, and this guide will share exactly what you can expect from the event so far.

IFA is the world’s biggest home and consumer tech event. Happening in Berlin, it hosts some of the world's leading innovative tech brands like Samsung, Acer, Anker, Eufy, Hisense and more, all gathering in one place to show off tons of cool, new, and interesting consumer gadgets and products. There's everything from gaming tech to home tech, and something exciting at every corner, no matter what you're into.

“Artificial intelligence is no longer just a promise,” says Leif Lindner, CEO of IFA Management. “Smart homes are no longer a vision. Digital health is becoming part of everyday life… The future is not waiting somewhere five or 10 years away. It is already in our homes, in our pockets, in our cars, in our health routines.”

AI and digital health is the theme of this year’s IFA, and the show promises to show more of how AI has “stopped being its own category and started becoming the connective tissue underneath everything else.” And yes, this also includes beauty, preventative health tools, connected fitness, wellness tech, and beauty devices, which signal consumers are looking for tech that “supports a more personalized, healthier daily routine.”

Speaking of personalization, last year's event brought in new robots that were very popular amongst attendees, including the KATA Friend AI pet shown below. There are new, impressive robots that people have never seen before at every show, and in nearly every category you can think of. Some are cute like this advanced digital pet, and others are more practical for every day routines and activities, including a stair-climbing robot vacuum or the Acemate Tennis Robot, the world's first AI-powered robot capable of true, real-time play.

Those in attendance or following along will be able to see these shifts and changes from the lens of a global CEO, a retailer, a startup founder, a content creator, a journalist, and a consumer, and it’s one of the few places that allows for these interactions to happen under one roof.

Furthermore, IFA will be more than just a showfloor, as it plans to utilize Sommergarter, the show’s open-air venue, to host BUNT’s electronic set on September 3, Luciano’s rap/hip-hop mix on September 4, Ikkimel & Friends bringing trap, techno, and Berlin club energy on September 5, and live podcast recordings from Mord auf Ex and Wine Wednesday on September 6.

The ICC Berlin, a protected 1979 landmark that has been closed for over a decade, will also reopen for IFA 2026, providing even more ways for attendees to engage and make the most of the opportunities the event offers.

You! But seriously, tech enthusiasts and general shoppers are welcome to attend. The event will have everybody from global owners to creators to startups to retailers in attendance. For more information, check out IFA 2026’s website, as well as the ticket information for BUNT, Luciano, and Ikkimel & Friends.

IGN will be in attendance at IFA 2026 next week and we look forward to seeing what new gadgets will go viral this year.

articles.title: Director of Marvel’s Wolverine Responds After Extended Gameplay Footage Sparks Backlash
articles.summary: The director of Marvel’s Wolverine, Mike Daly, opened up about the recent backlash toward the game after its extended gameplay showcase drew criticism online.
articles.body:
The director of Marvel’s Wolverine , Mike Daly, opened up about the recent backlash toward the game after its extended gameplay showcase drew criticism online.

Fans got a better look at Insomniac’s upcoming PS5 exclusive earlier this week, which showed off some story beats, character interactions, traversal, combat, and even a boss fight against a Sentinel.

Since the internet is the way it is, this gameplay footage was instantly subject to intense scrutiny, sparking no end of criticism from players online. There’s a bevy of viral posts poking fun at this most recent footage, some of which I’ve included down below.

Logan, remember to use your adamantium vision to sniff out his trail of wolverine™️ particles — Space ☆ Bruce (@spacebruce) August 13, 2026

Logan, remember to use your adamantium vision to sniff out his trail of wolverine™️ particles

Why does Sabertooth sound exactly like this pic.twitter.com/a5o46PpcZa — Deacon (@crowdeacon) August 16, 2026

Why does Sabertooth sound exactly like this pic.twitter.com/a5o46PpcZa

Logan following a red scent trail to catch The Hand was one major talking point among critics (instantly sparking comparisons to the divisive yellow paint that often guides players in modern games), as was a heated argument between Wolverine and Sabertooth (people weren’t happy with the voice acting here) and the aforementioned Sentinel boss fight.

One particularly damning tweet compared footage from this brawl to a boss fight in the 2007 PS2 game Ben 10: Protector of Earth (why is Ben 10 catching strays?), while another bemoaned that it was too similar to the 2009 X-Men Origins game from nearly 20 years ago.

Marvel Wolverine game's Giant Sentinel fight draws Ben 10 comparisons Many spot clear similarities to Ben 10: Protector of Earth, prompting complaints about overused boss designs in action games pic.twitter.com/bR21DsxAd7 — Beebom Gaming (@beebomgaming) August 14, 2026

Marvel Wolverine game's Giant Sentinel fight draws Ben 10 comparisons Many spot clear similarities to Ben 10: Protector of Earth, prompting complaints about overused boss designs in action games pic.twitter.com/bR21DsxAd7

X-Men Origins: Wolverine's Sentinel boss fight was way crazier and more interesting, while Insomniac Games designed a common, dull boss fight in Marvel's Wolverine. X-Men Origins: Wolverine is a 17-year-old game. 💀 pic.twitter.com/fTafQPMTi2 — Raion Sensi (@RaionSensi) August 15, 2026

X-Men Origins: Wolverine's Sentinel boss fight was way crazier and more interesting, while Insomniac Games designed a common, dull boss fight in Marvel's Wolverine. X-Men Origins: Wolverine is a 17-year-old game. 💀 pic.twitter.com/fTafQPMTi2

These criticisms did not go unnoticed. Speaking with TheGamer , director Mike Daly seemed to be at peace with the backlash, even welcoming it as a sign that the studio is doing something right.

In a somewhat concerning admission, Daly said that Insomniac is “pretty used to” these kinds of responses, calling it a “good problem to have” and remarking that such reactions “come with the territory” when making games based on people's favorite superheroes. And while he knows that Insomniac can make a “great game that a lot of people love,” it won’t stop critics from “finding stuff to complain about.”

“I rest easy about this, knowing that our goal for the game wasn't necessarily to accomplish these things that people complain about. Our goal really was to focus completely on making the best game for the character,” Daly said.

IGN also got the chance to sit down with Insomniac for a massive interview all about the game, with insights into combat, hardware performance, and much more. And while the general internet populace seems to feel negatively about what they’ve seen thus far, our hands-on with the game left us with a mostly positive impression.

IGN’s Mitchell Saltzman remarked that Wolverine’s combat “absolutely nails the spirit of Wolverine and is very fundamentally sound,” saying he was “impressed” with what he played, but noted that it’s still unclear if the gameplay will “hold up over the course of the entire campaign.”

Marvel’s Wolverine releases on September 15, 2026 exclusively on PlayStation 5.

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

articles.title: Steam Frame Seems to Be On the Horizon as Unboxing and Setup Videos Leak Online
articles.summary: After setup videos leaked online, Valve opted to push them out officially.
articles.body:
It seems like Valve may be gearing up to launch the Steam Frame, the third and final piece of hardware it showed us last year , alongside the Steam Machine and Steam Controller . Earlier today, a number of unboxing, setup and other how-to videos for Valve's upcoming next-generation VR headset leaked online via an update to the ARM Steam Client. Valve quickly pulled them down, but not before they were grabbed and re-uploaded by users.

Instead of pitching a fit – I'm sure the company was not psyched to have these videos leak before originally intended – Valve put the videos back up, and while it hasn't officially pushed them out yet, they're easily found in the Steam backend and can be found via the links collected here .

STEAM FRAME UPDATE: The ARM Steam Client had an update this morning that contained these videos. It was quickly pulled after that, but of course people managed to grab them. These are videos that detail the unboxing, sign-in, and setup of the Steam Frame. pic.twitter.com/AAFk5D69eJ — Steam Hardware Updates (@HardwareSteam) August 19, 2026

STEAM FRAME UPDATE: The ARM Steam Client had an update this morning that contained these videos. It was quickly pulled after that, but of course people managed to grab them. These are videos that detail the unboxing, sign-in, and setup of the Steam Frame. pic.twitter.com/AAFk5D69eJ

The videos detail how to set up and sign in to the device, which will require a Steam account to use. As a reminder, Steam Frame can be used as a standalone VR headset, or wirelessly connected to a PC running Steam. Other videos that leaked include things like how to install the head strap and light blockers, as well as one detailing the wireless adapter and a number of ergonomic accessories.

In his hands-on with the device last year, my colleague Michael Higham noted how Steam Frame gets you the same interface and quality-of-life features as the Steam Deck and Steam Machine, and noted how much he enjoyed using the device as a virtual theater to play non-VR games.

"This kind of experience isn't new," he said, "but the seamless integration through SteamOS also makes it very easy to use, and the super fast wireless tech means you can play PC games with the full strength of your system at low latency."

With these setup videos leaking, it seems likely that Valve is planning to launch the Steam Frame soon, which lines up with the plan to have it in customers' hands before the end of Summer 2026 . That said, we still don't know how much the Steam Frame will cost, but if the price of the Steam Machine (and hardware prices in general ) is any indication, it will likely end up being more expensive than Valve originally hoped .

For more on Steam Frame, check out our Q&A with Valve about why it's going back to VR, how the tech has evolved since the groundbreaking Index VR headset, and how it got wireless streaming to work so well.

Bo Moore is IGN's Senior Manager of Tech. You can find him online @usebomswisely.

articles.title: Former Tekken 8 Director Kohei Ikeda Joins VS Studio, Re-Teams With Tekken Veteran Katsuhiro Harada
articles.summary: The news likely won’t come as a surprise to hardcore fighting game fans.
articles.body:
Former Tekken 8 Director Kohei Ikeda has announced he has joined newly established developer VS Studio, the Tokyo-based, SNK-owned outfit that was founded in May 2026 by former Tekken producer and director Katsuhiro Harada.

“I’ve joined VS Studio as the next step in my journey,” confirmed Ikeda via social media. “Working on games again with two of my former bosses feels nostalgic in many ways, while at the same time, the excitement of creating something completely new makes every day incredibly fulfilling.”

“I’m really looking forward to seeing what we can create together!”

Ikeda left Namco Bandai back in June . His 20-year stint at the storied developer culminated with his duties as game director on both Tekken 7 and 8. At least according to Harada, Ikeda’s final direction on Tekken involved ensuring one of Harada’s own final requests came to fruition, which was his plan to tease the return of Roger Jr. by re-creating a 10-year-old viral clip out of Australia of a man punching a kangaroo to rescue a dog .

Ikeda’s exit came rapidly in the wake of Harada’s own departure following over three decades at Namco Bandai, after which the Tekken legend quickly founded VS Studio.

A glimpse at what VS Studio has in store is likely some way off, but it would appear there is no shortage of fighting game experience assembled at the new developer so far.

articles.title: The Audi S6 Sportback E-tron proves that sedans still matter
articles.summary: Sedans are back!
articles.body: Last year, Audi announced that it gave its all-EV-by-2033 plan the boot, and instead will offer a mix of gasoline, hybrid, and electrified propulsion. There’s no doubt still some uncertainty among bigger automakers — especially those under the Volkswagen Group umbrella — when it comes to such a (now prior) commitment. Even so, what it’s currently offering on the EV front is rather good, and fits into the German brand’s under-the-radar fast sedan tradition quite well. I recently discovered this in the 2027 Audi S6 Sportback E-tron. A cross between a sedan and a wagon in terms of its rearward shape, there’s no hulking Quattro all-wheel drive system to mess with chassis balance, just a motor on each axle, big battery in the middle, massive power output, and solid chassis tuning. Starting at $80,895, here’s how this electrified fast sedan formula shines. The Audi S6 Sportback E-tron rolls out with 800V architecture and a 100kWh (94.4kWh net) battery. Peak power is rated at 543hp and primarily comes from the rear motor, which enables a rip to 60mph in 3.7 seconds. Audi says it’ll charge from 10 to 80 percent in as little as 21 minutes, or 11.5 hours if it’s plugged into a 240V level 2 setup where juice is fed at 9.6kW. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Peak range is rated at 326 miles; by comparison, the comparable BMW i5 M60 will travel around 45 fewer miles, possesses 50 more hp, runs a similar 0–60 time, and costs a few grand more. During my stint in the Audi, I traveled 295 miles at an average of 2.4 miles per kWh, meaning I saw just 226.56 miles of range. A mighty difference, though; my average speed was just 19mph thanks to much of my driving staying within the Los Angeles basin, plus a handful of highway and mountain-road blasts thrown in for good measure. Much to my surprise, I saw its 270kW peak charging rate at my local Electrify America station during one visit, then as much as 194kW during another. For maximizing charge, the S6 has three levels of regenerative braking: Two are toggled via paddle shifters, whereas full-on one-pedal driving (OPD) is done by putting it in B mode. All three felt smooth, and OPD was just right; not too aggressive and able to smoothly slow down and stop in normal daily driving with ease. The S6’s seats and driving position were quite good, though rear-seat passengers may feel squished due to the Sportback body’s sloping roofline. Cargo volume starts at 26 cubic feet and maxes out at 39, and its large hatch makes loading and unloading easy. The lion’s share of my tester’s $13,595 in options mostly pertained to its added luxury and tech, like more luxurious Audi exclusive interior materials, plus a detailed heads-up display, upgraded exterior lighting, and a screen for the front passenger. Otherwise, the driver has access to Audi’s latest MMI via 14.5-inch center infotainment screen that’s a lag-free and easy-to-swipe-through experience. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Multi-link suspension with sport-tuned air suspension is standard on the S6 E-tron, as are 20-inch wheels with all-season tires. My tester sported the $2,000 Black Optic package, which gives it 21s with grippy Michelin summer tires — though there’s a good chance these knock a few miles off of its EPA-estimated range. Whether in the damper assemblies’ Comfort or Dynamic setting, ride quality was quite good over LA’s most brutal streets, and speed bumps were dealt with particularly well. The even firmer Dynamic Plus was solid and surprisingly agreeable, too. Squeaks and rattles over such cursed surfaces were negligible, though the same can’t be said for driveway clearance scrapes — luckily, there’s some reassuringly substantial plastic on the underside of the front bumper. But the real test came on LA’s freeway system, as that’s where any good fast German sedan should flourish — and the S6 did just that. Wind noise was virtually nonexistent, and it felt very well planted and confident. (It ought to be for weighing over 5,200 pounds.) In town, steering was too light, albeit nicely direct in its response, and thankfully it became more weighted at highway speed. The S6’s 16.4:1 steering ratio was well matched for its size and heft, and it never felt too darty while making split-second lane changes. It may be down on power compared to its BMW rival, but its numbers were still more than ample and its progressive powerband instilled confidence. Going way beyond the speed limit bolstered this confidence even further. Then, on the winding roads of Angeles National Forest just north of Los Angeles, the S6 behaved particularly well. Due to its chassis balance and rear-biased power output, there was never any inkling of understeer, which is characteristic among many Audis of yore. Its tires gripped up well and body roll was basically nonexistent in particularly lateral-G-heavy corners. With traction / stability control shut off, all signs pointed to the S6 being able to exhibit legitimately fun oversteer, which is a welcome trait. If only I could revisit such enthusiasm on a local racetrack. Finally, its brakes don’t look like much compared to rest of this hefty sedan’s dimensions, but they capably shaved off speed, especially with B mode aiding in the effort. Audi’s proven that the luxurious and fast German sports sedan formula applies to EVs, too, in the latest S6 Sportback E-tron. Over 300 miles of range (ideally) and good charging speed is a solid starting point, and its overall balance of comfort and athleticism makes it one of the best big fast sedans that I’ve ever driven.

articles.title: IDW Reveals a Bold, Colorful Future for The Twilight Zone
articles.summary: IDW's The Twilight Zone series has been extended for another story arc, and we've got an exclusive look at these stunningly colorful new sci-fi tales.
articles.body:
In 2025, IDW Publishing added a big gun to its IDW Dark imprint with the debut of a new The Twilight Zone series. Recently, the publisher revealed that the series has been extended for a new batch of six issues (taking the series up through issue #16), and IGN is pleased to be able to reveal new details and artwork from these upcoming books.

Check out the slideshow gallery below to see cover art for The Twilight Zone #11-14:

IDW's The Twilight Zone #11-16 Cover Art Gallery

True to the format of the classic TV series, each new issue of The Twilight Zone will feature a standalone tale from a different creative team. These new issues will feature a common thread, however, as each is presented in limited color rather than the traditional black-and-white. Each issue will feature one specific hue - green for #11, purple for #12, orange for #13, red for #14, yellow for #15, and blue for #16.

"This next volume of the Twilight Zone paints the human spirit in technicolor," co-editors Nic Niño & Ellen Boener tell IGN. "In stories ranging from extraterrestrial to intimately human, we face man-eating plants, giants, funeral rites, and family tragedy… Each cartoonist is taking full advantage of the color in their issue and never in the way you would expect! It’s changed the way artists approach the page; with everyone submitting career-best work."

Look for The Twilight Zone #11 to hit stores on October 21. You can preorder a copy at your local comic shop .

articles.title: The Strange New Worlds Puppet Episode Feels Like It Got Here 20 Years Too Late
articles.summary: The puppet episode of Strange New Worlds feels like it got here 20 years too late, with Ethan Peck’s non-puppet Spock standing tall as the hour’s saving grace.
articles.body:
Spoilers follow for Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 5, “Level Five Transporter Accident.”

Alright then, the puppet episode is finally here.

We’ve known this one was coming ever since it was first teased, what, two San Diego Comic-Cons ago ? The latest in high-concept Strange New Worlds episodes – this directly follows the zany Hangover riff from two weeks ago, and last week’s film noir homage – “Level Five Transporter Accident” certainly does feel like an accident… but not one that can be fixed with mere needle and thread the way the puppets here can. Indeed, its only saving grace is the performance from the always reliable Ethan Peck as Spock, who manages to walk the line between comedic Vulcan acting and conflicted Vulcan acting just fine.

When Scotty (Martin Quinn) tries to push his transporter tech to its limits – a nice nod to the Kelvinverse movies, where that Scotty (Simon Pegg) makes some big leaps with the old beam ‘em up technology – things go awry. Since he’s using his childhood puppet “Little Ricky” as a test subject, when the system gets screwy, somehow everyone onboard winds up beaming into puppet versions of themselves. And mostly annoying puppets at that.

I’ve complained about this before, but one of my issues with these Strange New Worlds concept episodes is that a lot of said concepts have been done before, if not ad infinitum , on other shows. The musical episode “Subspace Rhapsody” was great and all, but you know, not exactly an original idea . A film noir episode? Been there. LARPing with the crew? Mmmhmmm . And now we get a puppet episode, the idea of which I can recall seeing at least as far back as on Angel 22 years ago, when it felt like a new idea .

And look, there’s nothing wrong with recycling old premises, but if you’re gonna do it, you gotta bring something new to the table. It’s got to work, and “Level Five Transporter Accident” mostly doesn’t. For starters, by its very nature, the notion of having most of your cast turn into puppets is going to bring a heightened sense of absurdity to things; the characters even harness this idea in their quest to defeat the nasty if forgettable Orion villains of the week. But there’s something about suddenly hearing voices like Anson Mount’s and Christina Chong’s coming from the puppets that I found too jarring. It’s all supposed to be fun and funny, but it’s mostly not, and once again Mount’s take on Pike veers into “this is not a Starfleet captain” territory, wool stuffing notwithstanding.

So what does work here? I think I laughed out loud twice, and both times it was involving the guy at the navigation console next to Ortegas (Melissa Navia) who would usually have been a Red Shirt but instead here is just a funny puppet. His wordless panic about the situation is great. And the puppet designs themselves (created by the Jim Henson Company) are really nice – like, they should sell them on the Paramount+ store because people would want to collect them all. Oh, and the shots near the end of the episode, with the crew all floating around in space in puppet form, are just quite sweet (and really, is how the hour should’ve ended, instead of turning it into an “It was all a dream” scenario for some reason).

And then there’s the Spock stuff, which saves the episode from disaster. Peck’s comedic timing is notable, as he has to run around doing everyone’s jobs for them to keep the ship running, since their little puppet fingers are mostly useless. The actor really has mastered Spock – he and Mount have been playing these characters since 2019 at this point, when they debuted on Star Trek: Discovery – and he always rolls with the various curveballs the writers have thrown at him. Too Vulcan, too human, too Vulcan/human, he’s done it all, and here he’s dealing with not just getting dumped by another crewmate (though La’an was pretty graceful in the dumping, unlike Chapel previously), but also in having to go to his ex, T’Pring (Gia Sandhu), for help in the aftermath of the incident onboard the Griffin earlier this season. I’m glad to see they didn’t just drop that thread, and continuing to explore its impact on both Spock and La’an is welcome.

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

About it all being a dream… was it? Little Ricky sure seemed malevolent in that last shot… or maybe Spock just needs more logic training.

But what is this “studying logic” thing anyway? Hasn’t Spock been doing that since he was in diapers?

Could Little Ricky be a reference to the onscreen son of Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz from I Love Lucy? The puppet even has a red crop of hair on its head. Don’t forget, the pair’s production company Desilu was behind the original Star Trek series.

Pelia (Carol Kane) pointing out that they shouldn’t be able to hear each other in space and how it doesn’t even make sense is an appreciated jab at the grumps in the audience like me.

articles.title: New Fallout Funko Pops Are Dropping in November, Including Vault Boy, Nuka-Girl, and More
articles.summary: Preorders have dropped for new Fallout Funko Pop figures, which are set to be released this November. Priced at $14.99 a piece, here's where you can secure each figure.
articles.body:
Funko Pop is unleashing some new Fallout figures into the wild this year: Vault Boy , Nuka-Girl , Cappy , and Bottle . Priced at $14.99 a piece, each of these is set to be released in just a few months on November 22, just in time for the holiday season. If you're a big fan of the games (or maybe fell in love with them while watching the TV show ), these look well worth picking up to add to your collectibles.

As is the case with most Funko Pop figures, these are all fairly small (around 3.75 inches tall), so will slot nicely into an existing collection of Fallout-themed goodies. They each have quite fun designs as well.

While Cappy and Bottle are just happily posed with waving hands and big smiles, Nuka-Girl is pictured blasting off in a spacesuit with a ray gun, and Vault Boy is modeled with a classic thumbs up pose and a wink. The latter is a slightly different pose to the Vault Boy Funko Pop that released last year for the TV show , as that one was all wide-eyed smiles while posing instead of the wink.

While their release date isn't until late in November, it's worth preordering these now if one or more of them have caught your eye, rather than waiting. These kinds of figures can sell out faster than you'd think, so it's always a good idea to secure your favorites now before stock is all sold out.

If you're looking for even more Fallout items to buy for your shelves, we've got your covered. Our rundown of the best Fallout gear and collectibles highlights some of our favorite finds we think are worth your time, but the IGN Store is also chock-full of Fallout collectibles to look through. No matter if you've been a longtime fan of the games or just really love the show, there's a little something for everyone.

articles.title: Marvel Addresses the Greatest Flaw of Civil War 20 Years Later
articles.summary: In both movie and comic book forms, the greatest flaw of Civil War is that the conflict eventually ended. But thanks to a pivotal new series, that problem is finally being addressed 20 years later.
articles.body:
When it comes to modern comic book crossovers, few stories can rival Marvel's Civil War when it comes to impact and influence. There was rarely a more exciting time to be reading Marvel's comic book line than the summer and fall of 2006, as iconic heroes like Iron Man and Captain America battled it out on the page and Spider-Man made international headlines. You can take issue with Civil War's execution and the way it characterized certain key players, but the fun factor and the core appeal of the series' premise are undeniable. It's no wonder Marvel Studios adapted the series to great success with 2016's Captain America: Civil War movie.

There's just one problem with Civil War in both its original and MCU forms - its influence on the larger Marvel Universe eventually faded. The ideological conflict over superhuman registration faded without ever being truly resolved. But thanks to Avengers: Armageddon , Marvel is finally addressing that flaw 20 years later. Civil War is a story that arguably never should have ended, and now, it seems it never did.

Read on to learn more about how this new crossover has successfully revived the Civil War conflict two decades later, but beware of spoilers for Avengers: Armageddon #3 ahead!

Marvel Comics: Avengers - Armageddon Panel Image Gallery

Civil War certainly boasts a strong elevator pitch, if nothing else. The series explores what happens when the general public grows fed up with teams like the Avengers operating without governmental oversight. In the wake of a massive tragedy in Stamford, CT, a remorseful Iron Man leads the charge for the Superhuman Registration Act. Opposing him is his old buddy Captain America, who believes heroes need to be free to act without worrying about jurisdiction or jumping through procedural hoops. Personal freedom on one side, and security and accountability on the other. It was basically the perfect conflict for a post-9/11 Marvel Universe.

That ideological divide split the superhero community right down the middle, with some heroes flocking to Iron Man's pro-registration banner and others throwing their lot in with Cap's underground resistance. And perhaps the greatest success of Civil War is that it actually allowed one side (Team Iron Man) to triumph over the other. The Superhuman Registration Act became the law of the land in the Marvel Universe.

And, as MCU fans well remember, a similar conflict played out in Phase 3. Team Iron Man won the debate in Captain America: Civil War, leading to a new status quo where Cap and his allies became fugitives from the law.

But again, the issue with both versions of the story is that the effects of Civil War eventually faded. On the comics side, Marvel explored the long-term fallout of Civil War in subsequent crossovers like 2007’s World War Hulk and 2008’s Secret Invasion, with Iron Man eventually becoming disgraced and replaced in his role as S.H.I.E.L.D. director by Norman Osborn. In the end, Osborn himself was exposed and overthrown, leading to the general public accepting the return of a more traditional, registration-free Avengers team. After several years of turmoil, the Marvel Universe basically reverted to square one.

Similarly, the MCU no longer really feels the effects of Captain America: Civil War. The Sokovia Accords have been phased out, and the general public generally seems willing to accept the idea of heroes operating outside the law (see 2026’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day, where Tom Holland’s Spidey has become New York’s favorite darling despite being a one-man surveillance state). We’ve seen echoes of Civil War through plot points like Mayor Fisk’s anti-vigilante task force in Daredevil: Born Again, but that’s about it.

Frankly, it’s never made sense that the average Joe in either version of the Marvel Universe would simply forget about the idea of superhuman registration and move on. Is it really so unreasonable for ordinary civilians to expect a certain degree of transparency and accountability from these all-powerful super-beings? Does the fact that the Avengers saved the universe from Thanos in 2019’s Avengers: Endgame give them a permanent free pass? It’s never sat right that Marvel would just abandon the concept of superhero registration on either the comics or film side, rather than making registration a permanent part of the conversation going forward.

Marvel Cinematic Universe: Every Upcoming Movie and TV Show

Avengers: Armageddon - The New Civil War

Enter Avengers: Armageddon. This crossover has come on the scene 20 years after the original Civil War’s debut, and 10 years after the original sequel, Civil War II ( the less said about that book, the better ). Marvel isn’t actually calling this book Civil War III, but after reading issue #3, they might as well have used the name. This book is very much a spiritual sequel to the original Civil War, and I’m all for it.

In Armageddon, the Avengers again find themselves pulled between their responsibility to uphold the law and their duty as heroes. The series opens with Red Hulk and his gamma-powered soldiers invading the war-torn nation of Latveria and declaring it “New America.” The Avengers and Fantastic Four, along with Spider-Man, Wolverine, and former Captain America-turned-godlike hero David Colton, opt to respond to Red Hulk’s attack despite being expressly forbidden by the US government. That decision has caused a chaotic chain reaction of events that threatens to destabilize world peace and turn the public against the Avengers once more.

Colton himself is the architect behind much of that chaos, as he sets about unilaterally destroying the world’s nuclear stockpiles, Superman IV-style. Colton feels nothing but contempt for the Avengers, arguing that people with great power have the responsibility to use that power to make the world a better place. Meanwhile, a new wave of anti-Avengers resentment is brewing, with even Spider-Man questioning whether the world would be better off if superheroes faced more oversight. The series is putting a fresh spin on the same themes that were explored in the original Civil War, thereby proving that the argument over superhuman registration never fully went away.

As the series reaches its climax in issues #4 and 5, we’re going to see a real doomsday scenario play out. Already, Colton has sparked possible nuclear war by failing to eliminate every warhead in existence. Now Red Hulk has thrown his lot in with Russia’s Winter Guard, while the recently reconstituted S.H.I.E.L.D. has taken a stand against the Avengers and rebranded itself “Strategic Human Intelligence, Enforcement, and Logistic Defense.” There’s a world war brewing, and the Avengers are partly to blame.

It’s exciting to see a series finally pick up Civil War’s baton and carry it forward again. At long last, the concept of superhero accountability is at the forefront of the Marvel U. once more. Not in exactly the same way that Civil War presented it, but in a way that builds on that conflict and proves that the original story’s themes and ideas still very much resonate 20 years down the road.

And we already know the effects of this conflict aren’t limited to Avengers: Armageddon itself. This series directly sets the stage for Chip Zdarsky and Marco Checchetto’s relaunched Avengers comic, which sees a drastically different version of Earth’s Mightiest Heroes try to make a stand in a world that hates and fears them like never before.

Zdarsky teases that Spider-Man and his fellow Avengers will be very much dealing with the aftereffects of Armageddon and the question of responsibility in the new series, telling IGN, “Spidey is the poster boy for power and responsibility, so going into Avengers, he and every other hero are considering what that means."

I’m looking forward to a new status quo for Marvel’s comic book universe very much like the post-Civil War lineup in 2007, where heroes everywhere are forced to choose whether they can operate within the confines of the law. Everything we’ve seen of the upcoming Avengers comic suggests that this team will be underground fugitives, similar to how the New Avengers operated in opposition to Iron Man’s Mighty Avengers. That was easily one of the most creatively fruitful periods for the franchise of the past several decades. Why not draw inspiration from the post-Civil War Avengers line? There’s still so much material to mine there.

And, sooner or later, we can only hope that the MCU looks to stories like Avengers: Armageddon for inspiration. Just like the comics, it feels like there’s still so much room to explore the central ideas and conflicts that fueled Captain America: Civil War. Particularly with mutants like Sadie Sink’s Jean Grey now popping up, the general MCU public has to be growing more and more wary of the many unlicensed, unsanctioned superhumans running around. Rather than let the Civil War conflict fade into the background, there’s an opportunity to revive it and explore the sometimes tumultuous relationship the world has with its costumed defenders.

Civil War is nothing if not a great idea for a Marvel story. But like Pandora’s Box, once you open that lid, there’s no putting things back in order. Thankfully, Marvel seems to be belatedly realizing that fact in Avengers: Armageddon. The age-old battle between freedom and security rages on.

For more on the future of the Marvel Universe, learn all about the new symbiote hero known as The Amazing Venom and see what to expect from Kevin Smith's epic Star Wars/Marvel crossover .
